lead: M-ary FSK and QAM both send more than one bit per symbol. M-ary FSK picks one of M orthogonal tones; QAM picks one point on a two-dimensional grid of amplitude and phase. The first is simple and constant-envelope but uses wide bandwidth. The second is bandwidth-efficient but needs a linear amplifier and a cleaner channel. Telemetry, some military links, Wi-Fi, digital cable TV and microwave backhaul use these schemes.
prereq: You need: 6.1 ASK and FSK, 6.4 QPSK and M-ary PSK, and Unit 5 on signal space and the matched filter.

sections.h3: M-ary FSK: one tone per symbol

blocks.text: M-ary FSK sends k = log₂ M bits by choosing one of M carrier frequencies for T_s seconds. Each chosen tone is one symbol. The symbol rate is R_s = R_b / k, where R_b is the bit rate in bits per second and R_s is the symbol rate in symbols per second. The symbol time is T_s = 1 / R_s.

The M tones must be orthogonal over each symbol. For coherent detection, the minimum tone spacing is Δf = 1 / (2T_s). Then the inner product of any two different tones over T_s is zero. Noncoherent detection needs wider spacing, typically Δf = 1 / T_s.

The receiver is a bank of M matched filters or correlators. Filter i is matched to tone i. At time T_s each filter gives one number. The comparator picks the largest output. That index is the detected symbol, which maps back to k bits. The same idea appears in 6.1 for M = 2.

blocks.where: P_s is the symbol error probability; M is the number of tones; E_s is the energy per symbol in joules; N₀ is the one-sided noise power spectral density in W/Hz; Q(x) is the Gaussian tail probability. This is an elementary union bound for coherent orthogonal MFSK.

blocks.text: MFSK bandwidth grows with M. The M tones occupy a band of order M R_s, so doubling M adds one bit per symbol but roughly doubles bandwidth. MFSK is therefore a power-efficient, bandwidth-expensive scheme. Its constant envelope also suits nonlinear amplifiers.

Quadrature amplitude modulation, or QAM, sends data on two carriers in quadrature. The passband signal is s(t) = I(t) cos(2πf_c t) − Q(t) sin(2πf_c t), where f_c is the carrier frequency in Hz, and I(t) and Q(t) are the in-phase and quadrature baseband waveforms.

In square M-QAM, I and Q are independent √M-level PAM signals. For 16-QAM, each axis uses levels −3, −1, 1, 3. The point (I, Q) carries k = log₂ M bits. 4-QAM is the same as QPSK. 16-QAM and 64-QAM are common in Wi-Fi and cable modems.

items: Split the incoming bit stream into k-bit groups. Each group is one symbol.
Divide the k bits into two groups for the I and Q axes.
Map each group to a PAM level. For 16-QAM, use the four levels −3, −1, 1, 3.
Multiply the I level by cos(2πf_c t) and the Q level by sin(2πf_c t) in two balanced modulators.
Subtract the Q product from the I product and transmit the difference, I cos(2πf_c t) − Q sin(2πf_c t).

blocks.text: The coherent receiver uses two correlators, one with cos and one with sin. It recovers I and Q, then applies multilevel threshold decisions. For 16-QAM the I thresholds are at −2, 0 and 2; the Q thresholds are the same. A decision error on either axis can flip one or more bits.

blocks.where: P_s is the symbol error probability for square QAM; M is the constellation size; E_s is the average symbol energy in joules; N₀ is the one-sided noise power spectral density in W/Hz. The bit error probability is P_b ≈ P_s / log₂ M.

blocks.text: With rectangular pulses, the baseband null-to-null bandwidth is R_s, so the passband null-to-null bandwidth is B = 2R_s. The Nyquist minimum R_s / 2 needs ideal sinc pulses with zero excess bandwidth, which cannot be built. The bandwidth efficiency is R_b / B = k / 2 bits per second per hertz. For 16-QAM, k = 4, so the efficiency is 2 bps/Hz.

MFSK and QAM trade different resources. MFSK spends bandwidth to gain power efficiency and a constant envelope. QAM spends power and linearity to gain bandwidth efficiency. The table compares them for the same bit rate and the same M.

QAM fails badly if the amplifier compresses peaks. The outer constellation points move inward, so the received point lands in a wrong decision region. MFSK does not have this problem because every tone has the same envelope. The price is a wide band and many filters or correlators in the receiver.

A system designer chooses QAM when spectrum is costly and the channel has good signal-to-noise ratio. The designer chooses MFSK when the channel is poor, the amplifier is nonlinear, or noncoherent detection is needed.

figure.caption: A 16-QAM constellation on the I and Q axes. Each point is one symbol; the levels are −3, −1, 1 and 3 on both axes.

spec.aria: A 4 by 4 grid of 16-QAM points at I and Q levels −3, −1, 1 and 3.

examples.question: A 16-QAM system sends 20 Mbps over a 10 MHz null-to-null passband channel using rectangular pulses. Find the symbol rate, the bits per symbol, and the bandwidth efficiency. Does it fit?
steps: For 16-QAM, M = 16. The bits per symbol are k = log₂ 16 = 4 bits per symbol.
The symbol rate is R_s = R_b / k = 20 Mbps / 4 = 5 Msym/s.
With rectangular pulses, the passband null-to-null bandwidth is B = 2R_s = 2 × 5 MHz = 10 MHz.
The bandwidth efficiency is R_b / B = 20 Mbps / 10 MHz = 2 bps/Hz. This equals k / 2 = 4 / 2 = 2 bps/Hz.
The channel provides exactly 10 MHz, so the system fits with zero excess bandwidth.
examples.answer: 16-QAM carries 4 bits per symbol, runs at 5 Msym/s, needs 10 MHz null-to-null, gives 2 bps/Hz, and fits exactly.
examples.check:
import math
M = 16
Rb = 20e6
k = math.log2(M)
Rs = Rb / k
B = 2 * Rs
eff = Rb / B
print(k)
print(Rs)
print(B)
print(eff)

traps: Using M instead of log₂ M for bits per symbol. 16-QAM carries 4 bits per symbol, not 16.
Confusing E_s and E_b. The QAM formula uses energy per symbol E_s; E_s = k E_b. Putting E_b into the formula without converting gives a wrong error probability.
Treating M-QAM as M levels on one axis. Square M-QAM has √M levels on the I axis and √M levels on the Q axis, so 64-QAM has 8 levels per axis.
Assuming MFSK saves bandwidth because it uses many tones. MFSK bandwidth grows with M; it is a power-efficient scheme, not a bandwidth-efficient one.

Using the baseband bandwidth R_s / 2 as the passband null-to-null bandwidth gives the wrong efficiency 2k (8 bps/Hz for 16-QAM). The correct passband null-to-null bandwidth is 2R_s, which gives k / 2 (2 bps/Hz for 16-QAM).

quiz.q: How many bits per symbol does 64-QAM carry?
Why does the bandwidth of M-ary FSK grow when M increases?
quiz.a: More orthogonal tones are needed. Each tone needs a separate frequency slot, so the total band is of order M R_s. Doubling M adds one bit per symbol but roughly doubles the bandwidth.

quiz.q: A 64-QAM system sends 30 Mbps using rectangular pulses. Find the symbol rate and the null-to-null passband bandwidth.
quiz.a: k = log₂ 64 = 6 bits per symbol. R_s = 30 Mbps / 6 = 5 Msym/s. B = 2R_s = 10 MHz.

quiz.q: For 16-QAM, list the I-axis levels and the decision thresholds between them.
quiz.a: The I levels are −3, −1, 1, 3. The thresholds are −2, 0 and 2. A received I value is sliced to the nearest level.

quiz.q: Compare 16-QAM and 16-FSK at R_b = 20 Mbps. Which needs less bandwidth? Use R_s = R_b / log₂ M and approximate MFSK bandwidth as M R_s.
quiz.a: For both, k = 4 and R_s = 5 Msym/s. 16-QAM uses B = 2R_s = 10 MHz. 16-FSK uses about M R_s = 16 × 5 MHz = 80 MHz. 16-QAM needs much less bandwidth, but it needs a linear amplifier and a higher signal-to-noise ratio.

quiz.q: Why does QAM need a linear amplifier while MFSK can use a nonlinear amplifier?
quiz.a: QAM carries information in both amplitude and phase. A nonlinear amplifier compresses peaks and shifts outer constellation points, causing errors and spectral regrowth. MFSK carries information only in frequency; all tones have the same constant envelope, so amplitude distortion does not change the decision.

quiz.q: Write the symbol error probability formula for square QAM and define E_s and N₀.
quiz.a: P_s ≈ 4(1 − 1/√M) Q(√(3E_s / ((M − 1)N₀))). E_s is the average symbol energy in joules; N₀ is the one-sided noise power spectral density in W/Hz; M is the constellation size.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical QAM systems use adaptive modulation: Wi-Fi and 4G/5G change from QPSK to 64-QAM or 256-QAM as the channel improves. Peak-to-average power ratio and digital predistortion are major research topics for QAM transmitters. MFSK survives in low-rate telemetry and some underwater acoustic links where the channel is poor. Search next for “QAM PAPR”, “adaptive modulation and coding”, and “orthogonal MFSK spacing”.
